readings.title: The Brownies At School
readings.challenge: Notice when a character says one thing about himself and shows another.
readings.focus: A night in an empty schoolhouse turns into a game of taking turns at being teacher.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. Scholars here are pupils. In schools of the 1880s a rod or birch was a stick used to punish children, a slate was a small board for writing on, and a pupil who failed might be made to sit on the dunce’s stool. Disposition means temper or nature.
readings.contentNote: One Brownie describes the globe with words of the 1880s that insult the peoples they name (“savages,” “Hottentots”), and the Brownies play at punishing pupils with a stick, as teachers then did.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies at School,” the whole poem; opens “AS Brownies rambled 'round one night, A country schoolhouse came in sight; And there they…”; closes “…left open wide; And scholars knew, without a doubt, That Brownies had been thereabout.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the Brownies decide to go into the schoolhouse?
facilitatorNotes: The more they talk about it, the more they want to show how much they know. Curiosity and pride both push them in.
evidence: The wish to prove how much they knew.

questions.prompt: One Brownie says his friend is not fit to be teacher. What does he say a teacher needs, and does he have it himself?
facilitatorNotes: A kind disposition, patience, love and grace. He claims all of them while calling his friend a dunce with a bad temper, which is not very kind. Children enjoy catching the contradiction.
evidence: Should own a disposition kind.
Your place should be the dunce's stool.

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies settle who gets to be teacher?
facilitatorNotes: They take turns: each has an hour, then another takes “the rod of power,” because changes please the crowd.
evidence: And when one master had his hour,
Another took the rod of power;

questions.prompt: How do the children know, next morning, that Brownies have been in their school?
facilitatorNotes: Books are out of place, it takes an hour to tidy, and the windows are left wide open from the Brownies’ rush to hide.
evidence: The windows were left open wide;
That Brownies had been thereabout.

readings.title: The Brownies On Skates
readings.challenge: Follow a plan from idea to finish, and judge whether borrowing without asking is ever fair.
readings.focus: The Brownies take skates from a shop for one night on the ice and put back every pair.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. Three golden balls over a door marked a pawnshop, which lends money in exchange for goods and sells what is never collected; the broker is its owner. Club and rocker skates were kinds of skates in the 1880s; to muster is to gather; a mead is a meadow; Jumbo was a famous circus elephant of the time; scrolls are curling lines cut in the ice.
readings.contentNote: The shopkeeper is described only as “a native of queer, far-off lands,” a stranger seen through the prejudices of the 1880s. The Brownies enter the shop without permission.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies on Skates,” the whole poem; opens “ONE night, when the cold moon hung low And winter wrapped the world in snow And bridged…”; closes “…safely stowed away; Of their brief absence not a trace Was left within the dusty place.”.

questions.prompt: Where do the Brownies plan to get skates, and how do they get inside?
facilitatorNotes: From the pawnshop with three golden balls over the door. They slip in as easily as mice reach cheese, through a missing nail or down the chimney like Santa Claus.
evidence: Three golden balls hang by the door,
As mice can get to cake and cheese

questions.prompt: What goes wrong when they first try to skate, and why?
facilitatorNotes: The skates are far too big and stick out like spurs, so they slip and sprawl. The poem says people do the same the first time they skate.
evidence: Though far too large at heel and toe,
As people do, however nice,

questions.prompt: How can you tell the Brownies get better?
facilitatorNotes: They learn to curve, cut scrolls, race, jump, turn and skate backward, until a fall is rare.
evidence: But soon they learned to curve and wheel

questions.prompt: The Brownies take the skates without asking but bring every pair back. Is that borrowing or stealing?
facilitatorNotes: They return every skate and leave no trace, but no one gave permission. Children can argue either way from the poem.
evidence: With every skate that left the store.
Of their brief absence not a trace

readings.title: The Brownies’ Feast
readings.challenge: Keep track of many helpers doing different jobs at once.
readings.focus: Every Brownie fetches something, and together they boil and eat an enormous pudding in one night.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. A caldron is a huge pot; woodmen used this one for their forest work. A light is a windowpane; a plum pudding is boiled from flour, eggs and dried fruit, wrapped in a cloth; a repast is a meal; verdant means green; a stave is a stout stick.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Feast,” the whole poem; opens “IN best of spirits, blithe and free,-- As Brownies always seem to be,-- A jovial band,…”; closes “…wield a mystic power; Whate'er they take they can restore In greater plenty than before.”.

questions.prompt: What does each group of Brownies bring for the pudding?
facilitatorNotes: Flour from Parker’s mill, plums and currants, spice and sugar, the hens’ eggs (nest and all), and a sheet from someone’s clothesline to wrap it in; others build the fire.
evidence: And through the opening we'll pour
Had taken nest-egg, nest, and all;
From some one's line had hauled a sheet,

questions.prompt: Why has the farmer’s wife never found the hens’ nest, when a Brownie has?
facilitatorNotes: The hens cackle in other places to lead her away. The Brownie simply saw them sneaking out to lay.
evidence: I saw them stealing out with care
Until she quits them in despair.

questions.prompt: Some people think Brownies live on sweet smells. What does this poem show?
facilitatorNotes: They eat so much pudding that they can neither fly nor run. The poem makes a joke of the idea that fairies never eat.
evidence: Some think that Brownies never eat,
The rogues could neither fly nor run.

questions.prompt: The poem ends by saying the miller never missed his flour. Does that make the night’s taking all right?
facilitatorNotes: It claims Brownies can restore what they take in greater plenty. Some children accept that magic; others notice the poem says nothing about the eggs, the nest or the sheet.
evidence: The miller never missed his flour,
Whate'er they take they can restore

readings.title: The Brownies’ Circus
readings.challenge: Picture several circus acts and the small funny details inside each.
readings.focus: After the crowd goes home, the Brownies put on a circus of their own until dawn.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. The ringmaster announces the acts and keeps the horses running round the ring; a performer crosses a high wire without falling; fetters are chains; lax means loose.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Circus,” the whole poem; opens “ONE night the circus was in town With tumbling men and painted clown, And Brownies came…”; closes “…to open air, And off through lanes and alleys passed To reach their hiding-place at last.”.

questions.prompt: What does each Brownie want to be in their circus?
facilitatorNotes: One will handle the elephant, one will be master of the ring with the whip, and one will be a clown who keeps the fun going.
evidence: The elephant can take in hand;
For I'll be master of the ring
Another said, "I'll be a clown;

questions.prompt: On the high wire, some Brownies trust their toes. What do the others do?
facilitatorNotes: They hold on with their fingers in case they fall, and half the band crowds onto the one wire at once.
evidence: And thought that fingers, after all,
No less than half the Brownies there.

questions.prompt: How does the great elephant behave with the Brownies?
facilitatorNotes: It stands trembling, afraid to move, while the whole band walks across its back. Ask whether the elephant is having any fun.
evidence: He seemed afraid to move the least,
He stood and trembled in his tracks,

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies leave, and why can’t they stay?
facilitatorNotes: They slip out through every flap and tear in the tent as dawn begins, because Brownies must never be seen by day.
evidence: Till dawn began to paint the sky;
They made their way to open air,

readings.title: The Brownies’ Voyage
readings.challenge: Follow a plan from start to finish, and notice what the planners did not expect.
readings.focus: The Brownies build a ship in one night, sail for the islands, and are caught in a storm.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. A strand is a shore; a craft or bark is a boat; the hull is its body and the keel and keelson its backbone; halyards, shrouds, ratlines and guys are ropes; calkers stuff the cracks so water cannot leak in; to tack, veer and reef are ways of steering and handling sails; a gar is a long, toothy fish.
readings.contentNote: The Brownies take their building supplies without asking; in the storm they fear they will drown, and the ship is wrecked.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Voyage,” the whole poem (the story goes on in “The Brownies’ Return”); opens “ONE night, a restless Brownie band Resolved to leave their native strand, And visit…”; closes “…ship again;-- And on that island, roaming 'round, That Brownie band for years was found.”.

questions.prompt: Why do the Brownies decide to build a ship?
facilitatorNotes: They have often looked at the green islands out at sea and longed to sail there and ramble over them.
evidence: And longed for means to thither sail

questions.prompt: Cox says the Brownies swarmed over the ship “Like bees around their hive in June.” Why is that a good comparison?
facilitatorNotes: They are many, busy, and all working at once, each at his own job, the way bees do. Children can name the jobs: chopping, hewing, spiking planks, stuffing seams, bringing nails, canvas and rope.
evidence: Like bees around their hive in June.

questions.prompt: How do different Brownies act when the storm comes?
facilitatorNotes: Some are seasick or frightened; a few brave ones stay on deck, climb the masts, steer, and shift the sails.
evidence: Then some were sick and some were filled
So, some brave Brownies nobly stood

questions.prompt: What happens to the ship, and why can’t they build another?
facilitatorNotes: It runs straight onto the rocks and breaks up, though the Brownies reach land. Brownies are said to be unable to make the same thing twice.
evidence: Upon the rocks, a total loss.
Of making twice what once they've made;

questions.prompt: The supplies came from somewhere, but “It mattered little whence it came.” What do you think of that?
facilitatorNotes: The Brownies simply took what they needed. Some children will say that is stealing; others that Brownies are magic and play by their own rules. Cox does not stop to judge.
evidence: It mattered little whence it came,
Or who a loss of stock might claim;

readings.title: The Brownies’ Return
readings.challenge: Listen to an argument between a bold planner and a careful one.
readings.focus: Stuck on the island for years, the Brownies ride home on the backs of sleeping sea birds.
readings.context: Recap: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. In “The Brownies’ Voyage” they built a ship in one night and sailed for the islands, but a storm wrecked it on the rocks, and Brownies cannot make the same thing twice. A league is about three miles; to ween is to suppose; pinions are wings; fowl are birds; albatrosses, cranes, loons, gulls and gannets are large birds; Orion’s belt and Venus are lights in the night sky.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Return,” the whole poem, which ends the story begun in “The Brownies’ Voyage”; opens “ONCE while the Brownies lay at ease About the roots of rugged trees, And listened to the…”; closes “…is out of sight; And ere the lamp of Venus fades We all must reach the forest shades.”.

questions.prompt: What is the first Brownie’s plan for getting home?
facilitatorNotes: To creep up on the sea birds while they sleep, jump onto their backs at a signal, and let the birds carry them across the water.
evidence: An easy task for us to creep
And trust to them to bear us o'er.

questions.prompt: What worries the second Brownie, and how does the first answer him?
facilitatorNotes: That the birds might fly out to sea and drop them when their wings tire. The first says the birds always circle and then cross to the coast, and the rising wind will blow them landward anyway.
evidence: Suppose the fowl should seaward fly,
Will drive the fowl against their will.

questions.prompt: What happens when the Brownies jump onto the birds?
facilitatorNotes: The birds wake in fright with flapping and screaming; some are too sleepy to cheep; then they all fly off in the gale with the Brownies clinging to necks, wings and tails.
evidence: Then rose wild flaps and piercing screams,
Some seized a neck and some a head,

questions.prompt: How do the Brownies know they are nearly home?
facilitatorNotes: They see the peaks they used to climb, the bay their ship left from, and the very tree where they planned to build it.
evidence: The shady grove, the very tree

questions.prompt: The first Brownie says only cowards cling to safe plans. Was the second Brownie a coward?
facilitatorNotes: He says he has never shunned a risk; he only pointed out a real danger. Some children will say both were needed: the bold one to act, the careful one to think. The plan worked, but partly thanks to the wind.
evidence: Have shunned a risk that others met,
To shallow schemes that will not bring

readings.title: The Brownies’ Friendly Turn
readings.challenge: Notice how a group shares a hard job, and why helpers might not want thanks.
readings.focus: On a snowy night the Brownies haul a whole woodpile to the house of a parson everyone forgot.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. A parson is a church minister; fuel here means firewood; oxen are cattle that pull heavy loads; a trace is the strap a horse pulls by; a cornice is the ledge along the top of a wall; a pulpit is the stand a minister preaches from.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Friendly Turn,” the whole poem; opens “ONE night while snow was lying deep On level plain and mountain steep, A sheltered nook…”; closes “…if it came, But whispered: "We don't understand-- It must have been the Brownie Band."”.

questions.prompt: Why does the parson need the Brownies’ help?
facilitatorNotes: The people of the village fetched their own wood from the timber lot but forgot him, so he has none to keep warm.
evidence: The village parson they forgot.

questions.prompt: Why won’t the Brownies borrow oxen or horses for the job?
facilitatorNotes: The animals pull and haul all day and need their rest, so the Brownies will use their own arms instead.
evidence: But let them take the rest they need.

questions.prompt: How are some Brownies different from others in this work?
facilitatorNotes: Some are built for heavy loads and feel greatest half crushed beneath a log; slighter ones struggle with loads but are quicker at games and clever plans. Each has his own strength.
evidence: As when half crushed beneath a weight.
They far beyond their comrades ran.

questions.prompt: What does the parson see in the morning, and what does he do about it?
facilitatorNotes: Wood piled so high around his house that he can hardly see the sky. He asks God’s blessing on whoever did it, and his people whisper that it must have been the Brownies.
evidence: But little sky was left in sight!
It must have been the Brownie Band.

questions.prompt: The Brownies work all night, get frostbitten noses and sore hands, and never stay to be thanked. Why do you think they do it?
facilitatorNotes: They like to show skill and courage and to do a kindness; being unseen is part of being a Brownie. Some children will say helping felt good enough; others that they did enjoy the adventure.
evidence: To show both skill and courage here.
A chance to render service kind,

readings.title: The Brownies’ Fourth of July
readings.challenge: Find the details that show how people celebrated a holiday long ago.
readings.focus: The Brownies borrow fireworks from a locked building and celebrate Independence Day on a hill above the sleeping town.
readings.context: Palmer Cox’s Brownies are imaginary little sprites who come out only at night and take care never to be seen by people. Independence Day, the Fourth of July, celebrates the American colonies declaring themselves free of the British king in 1776. Roman candles, wheels, bombs, crackers and rockets are fireworks; a bust is a statue of a head and shoulders; “him who led his tattered band” and “the Father of his Country” both mean George Washington; a fusillade is many shots at once.
readings.contentNote: The Brownies help themselves to fireworks from a locked building, and several are singed and burned setting them off.

excerpt.locator: “The Brownies’ Fourth of July,” the whole poem; opens “WHEN Independence Day was nigh, And children laid their pennies by, Arranging plans how…”; closes “…roaming 'round; And with reluctant feet they fled When morning tinged the sky with red.”.

questions.prompt: What are children doing as the Fourth of July comes near?
facilitatorNotes: Saving their pennies and planning how to spend every cent on the celebration.
evidence: And children laid their pennies by,

questions.prompt: Where do the Brownies get their fireworks? Does a locked door stop them?
facilitatorNotes: From a building where fireworks are made; it is bolted fast, but Brownie lore gets them in, and they help themselves.
evidence: Before a building bolted fast.
And helped themselves to what they found,

questions.prompt: Which firework picture shines above all the others? Why might it be put highest?
facilitatorNotes: George Washington, the Father of his Country, who led the fight for independence; the holiday celebrates what he and his soldiers won.
evidence: The Father of his Country blazed.

questions.prompt: What goes wrong for some Brownies, and do they stop?
facilitatorNotes: Fuses they think are out flare up; they get stunned ears, burned fingers and sooty faces. Few are afraid, and they keep going till morning. Ask why Cox says plasters, bandages, would have been more useful.
evidence: Some plasters would have served the band
But few were there who felt afraid
